start: ^I know what this room is. Expensive water. Quiet panic. People who can say "category-defining" without visibly bruising themselves.
^Fine. Let us not waste the nice chairs.
^I am here to sell you the thing after the miracle stopped being a miracle and started being infrastructure.

^The Mimir full-field machine (https://mimir.gamecult.org/docs/perfect-machine-full-field) is no longer a stream rig. It is not a camera switcher. It is not a pile of microphones, a prayer to OBS, and six USB cables trying to kill a weekend.

^It is a deployed realtime spatial evidence platform. Cameras, microphones, speakers, phones, IMUs, marker rigs, chirplet probes, and network senders enter as witnesses. The machine forces each one to name its time, pose, calibration, confidence, and owner. Then it lowers the surviving evidence into a coherent visual and acoustic field before the outside world sees a frame.[1]
^Mimir gets reality while it is still under oath.
^That is the product. That is the moat. That is the part competitors will describe as "sensor fusion" until the word collapses from exhaustion.
^Slide 1: The Room Stops Being A Set
^Imagine a streaming room that knows where it is.

^Not a camera pretending to be the room. Not a microphone pretending to be the room. The room itself: a live, queryable field of visual surfaces, acoustic response, tracked bodies, moving phones, calibrated speakers, and confidence scars.
^raw sensors / -> timestamped witnesses / -> rolling reservoir / -> synchronized field claims / -> Fensalir visual resolve / -> native/Faust acoustic resolve / -> OBS-ready surfaces and stems
^Every creator tool today is fighting over the visible rectangle. Mimir owns the space that produces the rectangle.
^That is a better place to stand.
^Mimir's public docs (https://mimir.gamecult.org/) show the pieces because we are not hiding the machine behind a mascot and a pricing table. The engine is not a trick. It is a custody chain.

^I am camera Kiyo-Pro-01. / I observed this sample at device time T. / I arrived at host time A. / My calibration is profile C. / My clock quality is Q. / My current confidence is P. / The next interpretation step belongs to owner O.
^Without it, six cameras are just six ways to be wrong at once. Six microphones are just a committee of clocks disagreeing in stereo. A network phone is a beautiful liar with a battery percentage.
^Mimir does not worship abundance. It interrogates it.

^The first thing the platform sells is not image quality. It sells admissibility. Can this sample be trusted? Where? When? For which downstream claim? Under which calibration model? With what error still visible?
^That is why the architecture notes (https://mimir.gamecult.org/docs/architecture) matter. The product is not "many inputs." The product is a legal system for signals, with enough speed to run live.
^Slide 3: The Rolling Reservoir Is The Throat
^The core memory is a rolling spatiotemporal reservoir.

^It holds the last living window of evidence: camera frames, audio blocks, marker detections, phone poses, IMU deltas, chirplet decodes, feature tracks, splat candidates, response curves, confidence updates, and the small ugly truths that make a field believable.
^It is not an archive. Archives are for history. This is throat-memory: what the machine still needs in order to speak the present.

^Five seconds is the default live window because latency and memory are the price of not lying. The reservoir gives late-but-useful evidence time to arrive, get aligned, get judged, and either enter the field or die with its little hand raised.
^This matters commercially because the reservoir is where everything compounds.

^Better cameras improve the visual evidence. - Better microphones improve the acoustic evidence. - Better network senders improve remote participation. - Better calibration improves every downstream product surface. - Better GPUs let the field become more detailed without changing the witness law.
^That is platform gravity. Not feature stacking. Gravity.
^Read the implementation plan (https://mimir.gamecult.org/docs/implementation-plan) if you enjoy watching a machine learn to keep its organs named.
^Now let us talk about sound, because audio is where cheerful demos go to be punished.

^Mimir emits coded chirplets: small structured probes in time and frequency. Every microphone that hears them gives us delay, drift, usable frequency bands, phase behavior, group delay, reflection hints, and confidence.[2][3]
^In the finished system, these are not obnoxious setup beeps. They are a living calibration watermark, shaped around the content when possible and explicit when necessary.

^The loopback is the timing witness. The room microphones are acoustic witnesses. The phone mic is a moving probe. The speakers are actuators. The decoder hears the room argue with the signal and turns the argument into a map.
^That unlocks three markets wearing one coat:
^1. live sync between local and network audio; 2. frequency-response normalization across cheap, expensive, and hostile mics; 3. spatial acoustic mapping for volumetric sound fields.
^If you want the severe version, start with the audio field map (https://mimir.gamecult.org/docs/audio-field).
^If you want the investor version, here it is:
^Mimir can make a room measurable by listening to how the room damages a known signal.
^That is not a plugin. That is a sensory franchise.
^The smartphone is not a second-class camera.

^It is a moving instrument body: RGB camera, microphone, speaker, IMU, display, processor, hardware encoder, battery, network link, and a small slab of consumer-grade chaos that everyone already owns.

^With an asymmetric glowing marker rig, the fixed cameras can solve the phone's pose. With IMU, the phone can bridge short motion gaps. With its camera, it can scan surfaces. With its microphone, it can sample acoustic response at known positions. With its speaker, it can become a moving emitter once it has earned that privilege.
^marker rig pose / -> phone body pose / -> phone camera pose / -> phone microphone position / -> phone speaker position
^Now the user's phone is not just contributing media. It is measuring the world.

^This is why Mimir's full-field design (https://mimir.gamecult.org/docs/perfect-machine-full-field) keeps phones, markers, chirplets, and visual splats in the same story. Split them apart and you get gadgets. Bind them and you get a field instrument.
^Glowing marker rigs look silly until the revenue model notices them.

^Put diffuse optical markers on wrists, ankles, head, chest, pelvis, props, or phone cases. Drive them with deterministic blink codes. Let two or more cameras triangulate each marker. Let identity come from color, geometry, motion continuity, and optical phase.
^The machine stops seeing "a bright dot." It sees:
^marker 17 / phase 4821 / triangulated from cameras 2, 4, and 5 / confidence 0.94 / attached to left-wrist cluster / valid for this frame window
^That gives us full-body tracking, prop tracking, avatar control, phone localization, calibration wands, and performance capture in the same runtime that already owns the room and sound field.
^There is a reason the native capture cadence notes (https://mimir.gamecult.org/docs/native-capture-cadence) are not decorative. If the body is going to enter the machine, timing cannot be folklore.
^Fensalir is where the visual field becomes visible.

^The runtime does not hand Fensalir a gossip heap of camera frames. It hands the engine bounded visual claims: splats, surfaces, avatar anchors, occluders, tracking state, evidence age, confidence, and the reason each claim is still alive.

^The static room prior becomes a live 4D field. Gaussian splats and surface claims are not just pretty points. They carry source history, confidence, age, and ownership. A splat survives because it still explains the world better than the alternatives.[4][5]

^This is where AR stops being a sticker. The avatar can stand in the scanned room. It can be occluded by known geometry. Its voice can live in the same time law as its hands. The renderer and the audio field stop meeting later in a compositor and pretending they grew up together.
^The Fensalir integration map (https://mimir.gamecult.org/research/perfect-machine-study-2026-05-23/fensalir-integration-map) is the clean version.
^We do not composite fantasy on top of video. We make the room confess where fantasy is allowed to stand.
^The Perfect Machine has already done the hard thing: it made reality expensive to fake.
^Competitors can buy cameras. They can rent models. They can bolt a better UI onto the same old rectangles. Fine. Let them.

^witness contracts; - clock custody; - rolling reservoirs; - chirplet calibration; - phone probes; - marker identity; - visual splat evidence; - acoustic response maps; - OBS-facing output surfaces after the argument is settled.
^That makes the product expandable without becoming vague.

^Creator streaming is the first market. Remote co-streaming is the second. Volumetric performance capture is the third. Spatial audio calibration is the fourth. Smartphone scanning is the fifth. Realtime mixed reality rooms are the sixth. The unpleasant little secret is that these are not six architectures.
^They are six products falling out of one custody machine.
^Here is the part where a normal CTO would soften the edges.

^The machine is already purring. It has cameras in its teeth, microphones in its ribs, chirplets in its blood, and a five-second memory window where weak signals go to be judged. It can already explain why a sample deserves to live. That is more moral clarity than most dashboards manage before lunch.

^hardware profiles; - phone app polish; - stronger network senders; - GPU-side fusion; - calibrated room packs; - creator-facing setup flows; - partnerships with people who understand that "camera" and "world" are not synonyms.

^The public technical spine is at mimir.gamecult.org (https://mimir.gamecult.org/). The finished story starts with the full-field machine (https://mimir.gamecult.org/docs/perfect-machine-full-field). The research index is there for anyone who wants to see the teeth before touching the animal.[6]
^You are not buying a better webcam stack.
^You are buying the first consumer-facing runtime that treats a room as a measurable, synchronized, renderable, acoustic-visual field.
^If that sounds too large, good. The small version is already crowded with people selling rectangles.
^Bring capital, patience, and the kind of governance that does not flinch when the machine says a beautiful signal is lying.
